stem: What does ServiceNow Problem Management help an organization do?

options.text: Identify the cause of errors in the IT infrastructure that surface as related incidents
Restore service as fast as possible without investigating the cause
Fulfill catalog requests for hardware and software
Control the lifecycle of all infrastructure changes

rationale: Problem Management hunts the root cause behind recurring incidents and works to stop them coming back. It's the 'why does this keep happening' process, sitting behind the day-to-day firefighting.

distractor_notes.B: Restoring service fast without finding the cause is Incident Management's job.
distractor_notes.C: Fulfilling catalog requests is Request Management.
distractor_notes.D: Controlling change lifecycles is Change Management.

stem: How is a problem defined in ServiceNow?

options.text: The cause of one or more incidents
A pre-approved low-risk change
A request for a new service
A configuration item in the CMDB

rationale: A problem is the underlying cause of one or more incidents. You create one to chase down that cause and keep the incidents from recurring.

distractor_notes.B: A pre-approved low-risk change is a standard change.
distractor_notes.C: A request for a new service is handled through Request Management.
distractor_notes.D: A CI is a record in the CMDB, not a problem.

stem: Which statement best reflects the priority of the Problem Management process?

options.text: Identifying and resolving the root cause matters more than raw time to resolution
Speed of resolution always outweighs finding the root cause
Problems should be closed without any investigation
Problems exist only to track service requests

rationale: Problem Management is methodical: time to resolution takes a back seat to actually identifying and resolving the root cause. That's the opposite emphasis from Incident Management, which races to restore service.

distractor_notes.B: That's the Incident mindset; Problem deliberately prioritizes root cause over speed.
distractor_notes.C: Skipping investigation defeats the entire purpose of Problem Management.
distractor_notes.D: Service requests are tracked by Request Management, not problems.

stem: In the best-practice Problem Management state model, which sequence of states is correct?

options.text: New → Assess → Root Cause Analysis → Fix in Progress → Resolved → Closed
New → In Progress → On Hold → Resolved → Closed
Draft → Review → Approved → Implemented → Closed
Open → Awaiting Caller → Resolved → Cancelled

rationale: The redesigned problem state model walks New → Assess → Root Cause Analysis → Fix in Progress → Resolved → Closed, guiding the investigation from triage through root cause to a verified fix.

distractor_notes.B: New/In Progress/On Hold/Resolved/Closed is the Incident state model, not Problem.
distractor_notes.C: Draft/Review/Approved/Implemented resembles a change approval flow.
distractor_notes.D: Awaiting Caller is an incident On Hold reason, not a problem state.

stem: What is the purpose of the Assess stage of a problem?

options.text: To decide if the problem needs investigation.
To permanently close the problem
To order replacement hardware
To approve a change request

rationale: Assess is the triage gate: you weigh the scale, extent, cause, and effect to decide whether the problem warrants a full investigation before sinking effort into root cause analysis.

distractor_notes.B: Closing happens at the end of the lifecycle, not during Assess.
distractor_notes.C: Ordering hardware is a request action, unrelated to assessing a problem.
distractor_notes.D: Approving a change is a Change Management step.

stem: Which role is permitted to assess a problem?

options.text: problem_coordinator
sn_incident_read
catalog_admin
knowledge_guest

rationale: Assessing a problem is allowed for problem_coordinator (along with problem_manager, problem_admin, and admin) — the roles that actually drive the problem process.

distractor_notes.B: sn_incident_read is read-only incident access, not a problem role.
distractor_notes.C: catalog_admin manages the service catalog, not problems.
distractor_notes.D: knowledge_guest is a knowledge consumer role, unrelated to problem assessment.

stem: What must happen to move a problem from the New state to the Assess state?

options.text: The assess dialog's mandatory fields must be filled.
A change request must be approved by the CAB
The CMDB must be rebuilt
The caller must reply to an email

rationale: Transitioning New to Assess prompts an assess dialog with mandatory fields. Fill them in and the problem advances — those fields make sure the basics are captured before investigation.

distractor_notes.B: CAB approval belongs to Change Management, not the problem assess transition.
distractor_notes.C: Rebuilding the CMDB has nothing to do with advancing a problem state.
distractor_notes.D: Caller email replies relate to incidents, not the problem assess gate.

references.title: Add a field in the assess mandatory field dialog

stem: What is a workaround in Problem Management?

options.text: A temporary way to restore service without a fix.
The permanent fix that closes the problem
A type of configuration item
A mandatory CAB approval step

rationale: A workaround buys time: it temporarily restores service or reduces the impact of a problem while the permanent resolution is still being worked out.

distractor_notes.B: The permanent fix is the resolution, not the workaround.
distractor_notes.C: A workaround is documented guidance, not a CI.
distractor_notes.D: CAB approval is a change step, unrelated to defining a workaround.

stem: What happens when you communicate a workaround on a problem?

options.text: Related incidents are notified a workaround exists.
The problem is automatically closed
All related incidents are deleted
The problem is converted into a change request

rationale: Communicating a workaround pushes a notification to the related incidents that a workaround now exists, so the incident process can use it or pass it to affected users.

distractor_notes.B: A workaround is temporary; it doesn't close the problem.
distractor_notes.C: Related incidents are notified, not deleted.
distractor_notes.D: Communicating a workaround isn't the same as creating a change.

stem: What does a known error article document, and what is its main benefit?

options.text: The root cause and workaround of a problem
The approval chain for a change request
The list of CMDB identification rules
The on-call schedule for major incidents

rationale: A known error article captures the root cause plus the workaround so the same issue can be recognized and handled fast next time — deflecting incidents before they pile up.

distractor_notes.B: Change approval chains live in Change Management.
distractor_notes.C: Identification rules are CMDB / Data Foundations configuration.
distractor_notes.D: On-call schedules are part of major incident handling, not known errors.

stem: After completing root cause analysis and deciding a problem can be permanently resolved, what should you submit to implement the fix?

options.text: A change request
A new incident
A service catalog item
A knowledge_guest role request

rationale: Permanent fixes touch the live environment, so they go through Change Management. You submit a change request from the problem to implement the resolution in a controlled way.

distractor_notes.B: A new incident records a fresh disruption; it doesn't implement the fix.
distractor_notes.C: A catalog item fulfills a user request, not a problem's permanent fix.
distractor_notes.D: Role requests are unrelated to implementing a problem fix.

stem: What is the purpose of a problem task?

options.text: It lets the coordinator ask SMEs for root cause/fix.
It closes all related incidents automatically
It approves the change that fixes the problem
It publishes the known error to the portal

rationale: Problem tasks split the investigation into pieces. The problem coordinator uses them to pull in SMEs — assigning tasks to different groups or users — to chase down the root cause and a proposed fix.

distractor_notes.B: Closing related incidents is a separate action, not the purpose of a problem task.
distractor_notes.C: Approving the change is a Change Management activity.
distractor_notes.D: Publishing a known error is a knowledge step, not a problem task.

stem: What does assessing a problem task determine?

options.text: The feasibility of working on the task
The caller's satisfaction rating
The CMDB health score
The change request's risk level

rationale: Assessing a problem task is about judging whether the task is feasible to work on before committing effort — the same triage spirit as assessing the parent problem.

distractor_notes.B: Satisfaction ratings relate to incidents/requests, not assessing a problem task.
distractor_notes.C: CMDB health is a Data Foundations metric.
distractor_notes.D: Change risk is evaluated in Change Management.

stem: A problem task is best described as which of the following?

options.text: The smallest unit of work on a problem.
A duplicate copy of the parent problem
A type of change request
A CMDB relationship record

rationale: A problem task is the smallest unit of work toward completing a problem — a discrete chunk of the investigation that can be tracked and assigned on its own.

distractor_notes.B: It's a child unit of work, not a duplicate of the problem.
distractor_notes.C: A change request is a separate record type in Change Management.
distractor_notes.D: CMDB relationship records live in the CMDB, not Problem Management.

references.title: Life cycle of a problem task

stem: Why would you categorize a problem as a major problem?

options.text: To prioritize and flag for review.
To delete it from the system
To convert it into an incident
To hide it from all reports

rationale: Flagging a problem as major bumps its priority and signals that it warrants a review — making sure the heaviest-hitting problems get the attention they need.

distractor_notes.B: Categorizing doesn't delete the problem.
distractor_notes.C: Problems and incidents are distinct; categorizing as major doesn't convert it.
distractor_notes.D: Marking it major surfaces it for attention, not hides it.

references.title: Categorize a problem as a major problem

stem: Following ITIL guidelines, problem records are prioritized based on what?

options.text: The impact and urgency of the problem
The number of attached knowledge articles
The order in which problems were created
The assigned group's headcount

rationale: Just like incidents, problems are prioritized from impact and urgency — typically via a data lookup — so the most consequential problems rise to the top.

distractor_notes.B: Attached articles don't drive problem priority.
distractor_notes.C: Creation order isn't the basis for priority.
distractor_notes.D: Team size has nothing to do with how a problem is prioritized.

stem: How can you automate sending a newly logged problem to the appropriate group or individual?

options.text: Define assignment rules for problems
Set the problem to On Hold
Create a known error article
Run CMDB Discovery

rationale: Assignment rules automate routing: once a problem is logged, the rule sends it to the right group or person based on predefined conditions, so it doesn't sit unassigned.

distractor_notes.B: On Hold is an incident pause state and doesn't route a problem.
distractor_notes.C: A known error documents cause and workaround; it doesn't assign the problem.
distractor_notes.D: Discovery populates the CMDB; it doesn't assign problems.

references.title: Define an assignment rule for problems

stem: Why would you add multiple incidents to a single problem?

options.text: To avoid multiple problems for the same issue.
To increase the problem's reopen count
To grant the caller the itil role
To bypass root cause analysis

rationale: If many incidents stem from one cause, you attach them to a single problem rather than spinning up duplicate problems — one investigation covers them all.

distractor_notes.B: Reopen count is an incident metric, unrelated to attaching incidents to a problem.
distractor_notes.C: Linking incidents doesn't grant roles.
distractor_notes.D: Grouping incidents supports root cause analysis; it doesn't bypass it.

references.title: Add multiple incidents to a problem

stem: Why might you add multiple change requests to a single problem?

options.text: To capture all changes needed for the fix.
To merge the problem into the CMDB
To auto-close all related incidents without resolution
To reset the problem to the New state

rationale: Some fixes take more than one change. Attaching multiple change requests to the problem captures the full set of changes required to resolve it, all in one place.

distractor_notes.B: Attaching changes doesn't merge the problem into the CMDB.
distractor_notes.C: Closing incidents without resolution isn't the purpose of linking changes.
distractor_notes.D: Linking changes doesn't reset the problem state.

references.title: Add multiple change requests to a problem

stem: What is the benefit of associating multiple CIs with a problem?

options.text: To find all CIs affected by the problem.
To recalculate each CI's purchase cost
To delete unused CIs from the CMDB
To assign the problem to the CMDB owner

rationale: Linking the affected and impacted CIs to a problem shows the full footprint — every configuration item touched by the same underlying issue — which sharpens impact analysis.

distractor_notes.B: Cost recalculation isn't a function of associating CIs with a problem.
distractor_notes.C: Associating CIs doesn't delete anything from the CMDB.
distractor_notes.D: It maps affected CIs; it doesn't reassign ownership.

stem: What is the effect of a change to a problem record on its related incident records?

options.text: Related incidents are impacted and notified per update.
Related incidents are permanently deleted
Nothing — problems and incidents are never linked
The CMDB is rebuilt

rationale: Problem and incident records are connected, so updating the problem ripples to its related incidents and fires a notification for each update — keeping everyone working the issue in the loop.

distractor_notes.B: Updates notify related incidents; they don't delete them.
distractor_notes.C: Problems and incidents are explicitly linked in this synchronization.
distractor_notes.D: The CMDB isn't rebuilt by a problem update.

references.title: Synchronization between incident and problem records

stem: How many options does the Problem form provide for creating knowledge and communicating information?

options.text: Four
One
Seven
Zero

rationale: The Problem form offers four options for creating knowledge and sharing information, giving the team several ways to turn what they learned into reusable content.

distractor_notes.B: There's more than a single option — four are provided.
distractor_notes.C: Seven overstates it; the documented count is four.
distractor_notes.D: The form does provide knowledge options, so zero is wrong.

stem: Regarding knowledge creation from a problem, which statement is true?

options.text: You can create a KB article before the problem closes.
A knowledge article can only be created after the problem is closed
Knowledge articles cannot be created from problems
Only an incident can generate a knowledge article

rationale: You don't have to wait for closure — you can post a knowledge article straight from the problem as soon as you have something worth sharing, so insights spread while they're fresh.

distractor_notes.B: Knowledge can be posted immediately, not only after closure.
distractor_notes.C: Problems can absolutely generate knowledge articles.
distractor_notes.D: Both incidents and problems can produce knowledge articles.

stem: When resolving and completing a problem, what is a recommended practice?

options.text: Add a resolution note for reference.
Delete the problem record
Remove all related incidents
Clear the root cause field

rationale: Capturing a detailed resolution note pays dividends later: it documents exactly how the problem was solved so future incidents on the same issue can be handled quickly.

distractor_notes.B: Deleting the record throws away the history and the lesson learned.
distractor_notes.C: Related incidents stay linked for traceability.
distractor_notes.D: The root cause is exactly what you want to keep, not clear.

stem: What do Problem Management models let you do?

options.text: Tailor processes with custom states/transitions.
Replace the CMDB with a flat table
Disable all notifications globally
Auto-approve every change request

rationale: Problem Management models let you craft custom states and transitions, so the process can flex to fit different kinds of problems rather than forcing one rigid flow.

distractor_notes.B: Models tailor the problem process; they don't touch the CMDB structure.
distractor_notes.C: Models don't globally disable notifications.
distractor_notes.D: Change approvals are governed by Change Management, not problem models.

stem: What must you do before you can create and use custom Problem Management models?

options.text: Enable the Problem Management models property.
Delete the default problem state model
Grant every user the admin role
Disable the CMDB

rationale: Custom models are gated behind a system property — enable Problem Management models first, and then you can build and use models with your own states and transitions.

distractor_notes.B: You don't delete the default model; you enable the models capability.
distractor_notes.C: Handing everyone admin is both unnecessary and unsafe.
distractor_notes.D: Disabling the CMDB is unrelated and would break far more than problem models.

stem: What does creating a problem model allow you to define?

options.text: Custom states and transitions.
The company's financial year
The MID Server cluster size
The Service Portal theme

rationale: A problem model is where you define the custom states and transitions for a particular use case, letting different problem types follow flows that actually fit them.

distractor_notes.B: Financial year settings are unrelated to problem models.
distractor_notes.C: MID Server configuration is discovery infrastructure.
distractor_notes.D: Portal theming is UI configuration, not a problem model.

stem: Which kind of behavior is controlled by Problem Management properties?

options.text: Whether you can create a problem task on a closed problem
The color palette of the Next Experience chrome
The number of CIs in a dynamic CI group
The SLA pause schedule for changes

rationale: Problem properties toggle process behaviors like allowing a problem task on a closed problem and reanalyzing a closed or canceled problem — the switches that shape how your problem process behaves.

distractor_notes.B: Chrome colors are a UI theming concern, not a problem property.
distractor_notes.C: Dynamic CI group limits are a CMDB setting.
distractor_notes.D: SLA pause schedules are configured in SLA definitions, not problem properties.

stem: Why configure problem categories and subcategories?

options.text: A refined way to monitor and report on problems.
To calculate the change risk score
To grant ESS users admin rights
To replace the problem state model

rationale: Categories and subcategories give you cleaner buckets for monitoring and reporting — so you can spot patterns and trends across your problems instead of one undifferentiated pile.

distractor_notes.B: Change risk scoring is a Change Management concern.
distractor_notes.C: Categories don't grant any roles.
distractor_notes.D: Categories classify problems; they don't replace the state model.

stem: Configuring Problem Management commonly includes which of the following activities?

options.text: Data lookup/assignment rules auto-assign the task.
Designing CSDM service models
Building MID Server clusters
Writing Service Graph Connector transforms

rationale: Setting up Problem Management involves shaping form layouts, categories, and — importantly — data lookup and assignment rules that auto-assign work based on conditions you define.

distractor_notes.B: CSDM service modeling is Data Foundations work, not Problem configuration.
distractor_notes.C: MID Server clusters are discovery infrastructure.
distractor_notes.D: Service Graph Connector transforms are ingestion configuration.

stem: The service desk notices the same network outage symptom generating dozens of incidents week after week. What should be created to find and eliminate the underlying cause?

options.text: A problem
A standard change
A service request
A new SLA definition

rationale: Recurring incidents from one root cause is the textbook trigger for a problem. You raise a problem to investigate the cause and stop the incidents at the source.

distractor_notes.B: A standard change implements a pre-approved fix; it doesn't investigate a recurring cause.
distractor_notes.C: A service request handles user asks, not recurring incident root causes.
distractor_notes.D: An SLA defines response/resolution targets; it doesn't find root causes.

stem: You've found a temporary way to keep a service running while the permanent fix is still unknown. What should you document and communicate on the problem?

options.text: A workaround
A resolution code
A close notes entry that closes the problem
A new caller record

rationale: A temporary measure that keeps service going while you chase the real fix is a workaround. Documenting and communicating it tells related incidents and users that relief is available.

distractor_notes.B: A resolution code is for when the problem is actually resolved, not a temporary measure.
distractor_notes.C: Closing the problem would be premature — there's no permanent fix yet.
distractor_notes.D: Caller records belong to incidents, not problem workarounds.

stem: Root cause analysis is complete and the permanent fix requires modifying a production server in a controlled way. What should you create from the problem?

options.text: A change request
Another problem
A knowledge_guest role
A duplicate incident

rationale: Modifying production safely is exactly what Change Management is for, so you create a change request from the problem to implement the permanent fix under proper control.

distractor_notes.B: You already have the problem and its root cause; another problem adds nothing.
distractor_notes.C: A role request doesn't implement a production fix.
distractor_notes.D: A duplicate incident records a symptom; it doesn't implement the fix.

references.title: Create change request from a problem

stem: A problem investigation is too large for one team, and the coordinator wants different subject matter experts across several groups to each handle a piece. What should be created?

options.text: Problem tasks assigned to the groups.
A separate problem for each group
A major incident
A service catalog item

rationale: Problem tasks let the coordinator split the investigation and assign pieces to different SME groups, all while keeping everything tied to the one parent problem.

distractor_notes.B: Spawning a problem per group fragments the investigation and duplicates effort.
distractor_notes.C: A major incident is about a live high-impact outage, not splitting a problem investigation.
distractor_notes.D: A catalog item fulfills user requests, unrelated to investigating a problem.

stem: Why is documenting the cause and resolution (the outcome) of a problem valuable?

options.text: It resolves incidents fast and prevents duplicate problems.
It automatically upgrades the instance to the next release
It deletes the related incidents
It disables the CMDB health dashboard

rationale: Writing down the cause and resolution turns a solved problem into a fast lane for the future — incoming incidents on the same issue get handled quickly, and duplicate problems don't get raised.

distractor_notes.B: Documenting an outcome has nothing to do with release upgrades.
distractor_notes.C: It informs incident handling; it doesn't delete incidents.
distractor_notes.D: It doesn't touch the CMDB health dashboard.

references.title: Communicating the outcome of a problem

stem: Which of the following are states in the best-practice Problem Management state model?

options.text: New
Root Cause Analysis
Fix in Progress
Awaiting Caller
Implementation

rationale: New, Root Cause Analysis, and Fix in Progress are genuine problem states (alongside Assess, Resolved, and Closed). Awaiting Caller is an incident On Hold reason, and Implementation isn't a baseline problem state.

distractor_notes.D: Awaiting Caller is an incident On Hold reason, not a problem state.
distractor_notes.E: Implementation isn't a state in the baseline problem state model.
